posts.title: Why We're Leaving America
posts.author: Brent & Denise
posts.alt: A map showing the US and potential destination countries with pins marking Costa Rica, Portugal, and Thailand
posts.excerpt: We spent years watching our savings buy less each year. Here is the evening we finally asked whether we had to stay, and what we decided.
posts.content:
The decision built up slowly. For years we watched grocery bills climb, property taxes rise, and our retirement accounts lag behind inflation. One evening we sat down with the spreadsheet we had opened a hundred times before and asked a different question: what if we didn't stay?

That question took us to countries where our savings stretch further, where healthcare is affordable, where a couple can live well on what we have built over forty years. The more we read, the more obvious the answer looked.

We know it surprises people. Our kids needed time to get used to it. Friends have called us brave and crazy in the same conversation.

Once you see a path to a retirement where money is not the first thing on your mind every morning, and there is room for the adventure we have been putting off, it is hard to stop seeing it. This blog is how we will document the move, share what we learn, and answer the question other people our age are already asking.

posts.title: Our Retirement Timeline: The Countdown Begins
posts.author: Brent & Denise
posts.alt: A calendar with dates circled and a plane icon marking December 2027
posts.excerpt: Denise has a date locked in. Brent is five years behind. Here is the plan that makes two retirements work on one timeline.
posts.content:
Denise retires in December 2027. She has given HR the date. After thirty-two years in public education she is ready to trade lesson plans for travel plans, and her pension vests fully at the end of that calendar year. She is giving the school maximum notice, but that last day is circled in red on our kitchen calendar.

My timeline runs later. I turn sixty in 2031, and my Social Security benefit nearly doubles if I wait for full retirement age. So Denise moves first, once we settle on a country, and I follow when the consulting work winds down. We will do long distance for a while and visit every six to eight weeks. Run the numbers and the staggered approach adds about twenty-three hundred dollars a month to our combined benefits, which matters on a fixed income.

Between now and her last day we are in preparation mode: downsizing the house, selling the second car, sorting through thirty years of accumulated stuff. The goal is to cut our monthly overhead by at least forty percent before she gets on a plane. Every dollar we cut now is a dollar we do not have to worry about later. The countdown feels more exciting than scary.

posts.title: Top 5 Countries We're Considering for Retirement
posts.author: Brent & Denise
posts.alt: A world map with five highlighted regions: Western Europe, Central America, Southeast Asia, and Southern Europe
posts.excerpt: Five countries check our boxes: affordable healthcare, a reasonable cost of living, safety, and a visa path built for retirees. Here is the shortlist and what each one costs.
posts.content:
Portugal has been at the top of our list from the start. The D7 passive income visa is straightforward for retirees with a modest pension, the healthcare system ranks among the best in Europe, and a couple can live comfortably in the Algarve or on the Silver Coast for around two thousand dollars a month. The climate is mild year round and English is widely spoken, which gives us time to learn Portuguese.

Costa Rica offers something different. It is close to the US, it has a long-established expat community, and permanent residents can join the universal healthcare system after a waiting period. The pensionado visa requires proof of just one thousand dollars a month in lifetime income. We could fly home for family events, and the country's biodiversity appeals to us. The cost of living is higher than our other options.

Panama runs on the US dollar, so there is no currency risk, and its Pensionado visa grants permanent residency along with discounts on medical bills, utilities and more. Boquete has a large retiree community and a spring-like climate all year. Malaysia's MM2H program and Thailand's retirement visa complete the list. Both run twelve to fifteen hundred dollars a month for a comfortable life, and private healthcare costs a fraction of US prices.

We are planning a scouting trip in early 2027 to visit at least three of them. Each one has trade-offs, and we want to see them before we decide where the rest of our lives happen.

posts.title: How Much Does It Really Cost to Live Abroad?
posts.author: Brent & Denise
posts.alt: A comparison chart showing monthly expenses in US dollars across different countries
posts.excerpt: We ran the numbers on rent, groceries, utilities, healthcare and dining out. The gap between the US and our shortlisted countries is larger than we expected.
posts.content:
We have tracked our monthly expenses for two years to build an honest comparison. Our budget in suburban Ohio runs about forty-eight hundred dollars a month: mortgage, two car payments, groceries, utilities, health insurance premiums, and the usual household costs. In Portugal, a two-bedroom apartment in a midsize city runs seven to nine hundred euros. Groceries for two average three hundred fifty euros. Private health insurance with good coverage runs about one hundred fifty euros per person per month. Our projected monthly budget there lands near twenty-two hundred euros, less than half of what we spend now.

Southeast Asia is cheaper still. In Chiang Mai, a modern furnished apartment costs around four hundred fifty dollars. Eating out at local restaurants runs two to three dollars a meal. A couple can live on under fifteen hundred dollars a month, including private insurance. The trade-off is distance from family and the need for reliable internet if we work remotely or stay connected back home.

Healthcare deserves its own paragraph. Our US plan costs twelve hundred dollars a month in premiums with a six-thousand-dollar deductible. Portugal's national health system is available to residents for a nominal fee, and private coverage for both of us runs about eighteen hundred dollars a year. In Thailand, top-tier international coverage that includes evacuation insurance runs roughly two thousand dollars annually. These are established systems serving millions of expatriates, not exotic arrangements.

Moving abroad is not for everyone. But if you are retired or close to it and watching your budget shrink every year, the numbers deserve a serious look. We built a detailed spreadsheet with a line item for every expense category and will share a downloadable version in a future post.
